alt: Solids have a fixed shape and volume, do not flow and are almost incompressible; liquids take the shape of their container, have a fixed volume and flow; gases fill their container, flow and are easily compressed. Melting turns solid to liquid and solidification reverses it; boiling or evaporation turns liquid to gas and condensation reverses it.
caption: Four named changes of state link the three states.

alt: Gas particles in a box move fast and randomly; one rebounds from the right-hand wall and pushes on it. Many collisions each second produce the pressure; more frequent or harder collisions give a larger pressure. For Extended, the force from the collisions divided by the wall area is the pressure.
caption: Pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls, not with each other.

alt: Smoke in a small glass cell is lit from the side and viewed through a microscope. Each smoke particle appears as a bright speck moving in a random, jerky, zigzag path. Fast-moving air molecules, too small to see, hit it unevenly from all sides, so the net push keeps changing direction.
caption: Uneven hits from invisible, fast-moving molecules jostle the visible smoke particles.

after: ## Gases and the absolute scale of temperature (2.1.3)
alt: Three boxes of the same gas particles: heated at constant volume they move faster and hit the walls more often and harder; squeezed into a smaller volume at constant temperature they hit each unit area more often. Both raise the pressure. Below, a °C scale beside a kelvin scale: −273 °C is 0 K, −196 °C is 77 K, 0 °C is 273 K, 37 °C is 310 K and 100 °C is 373 K.
caption: Hotter or squeezed, the walls are hit more often: higher pressure. Add 273 to convert °C to K.

after: ## Gases and the absolute scale of temperature (2.1.3)
alt: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, p against V is a falling curve that never meets the axes, through (60 cm³, 100 kPa) and (24 cm³, 250 kPa); p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin. In the syringe example 100 × 60 = p₂ × 24 gives 250 kPa; a 2.0 cm³ bubble at 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa becomes 6.0 cm³ at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
caption: Halve the volume and the pressure doubles; p against 1/V is a straight line.
